questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What counts as an urban place
questions.learningObjective: Define what counts as an urban place

stimulus.body: Source note: An urban place is defined by population density and built-up land. This is the claim the evidence in the topic supports.

questions.stem: A document on what counts as an urban place reads: "An urban place is defined by population density and built-up land" Using that evidence, a settlement has high density and built-up land; does it count as urban?

options.text: Any settlement with a mayor counts as urban.
An urban place is defined by population density and built-up land.
Only national capitals are urban.
Rural villages with farms are urban.

questions.explanation: Urban status usually depends on density and built-up land, not on governance, capital status, or rural functions. A village with farms remains rural.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Urban area and metropolitan area
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish urban area from metropolitan area
questions.stem: A map shows contiguous built-up land and a wider commuting zone; which is the metropolitan area?

options.text: They are always the same boundary.
Metropolitan area excludes suburbs.
Urban area is contiguous built-up land; metropolitan area includes commuting ties.
Urban area includes all commuting zones.
options.misconception: reads the evidence as Urban area includes all commuting zones instead of Urban area is contiguous built-up land; metropolitan area….

questions.explanation: The urban area covers contiguous built-up land, while the metropolitan area adds commuting and economic ties. They are not automatically the same.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Boundary and footprint on a municipal map
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish boundary from footprint on a map
questions.stem: A municipal map shows a city boundary and a built-up footprint; how do they differ?

answer.exemplar: The boundary marks legal jurisdiction, while the footprint shows the actual built-up land, so a city can have a large legal area with a smaller physical footprint.

questions.explanation: Legal boundaries and physical footprints often differ. The boundary sets jurisdiction, while the footprint shows where development actually occurs.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Primate city and the primacy it implies
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a primate city is
questions.stem: The largest city has 4 million people and the second has 1 million; compute the primacy ratio.
questions.explanation: Divide 4 million by 1 million to get 4. A ratio this large suggests strong primate-city dominance.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Average annual urban growth rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain average annual urban growth rate

stimulus.body: A clinician's note records an urban population rising from 100000 to 160000 over 5 years. The note asks for the average annual growth rate.

questions.stem: A document on average annual urban growth rate reads: "It is the compound annual rate that links initial and final populations" Using that evidence, which formula is correct?

options.text: It ignores starting population.
options.misconception: omits base population in growth rate

options.text: It is simple division of total growth by years.
options.misconception: uses simple instead of compound growth

options.text: It is always the same as birth rate.
options.misconception: confuses urban growth with natural increase

options.text: It is the compound annual rate that links initial and final populations.

questions.explanation: Average annual growth uses compound growth between the initial and final populations. Simple division or birth rate alone would misstate the rate.
questions.hint: Use compound growth over the period.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Testing a rank-size pattern against a table
questions.learningObjective: Test a rank-size pattern against a table

stimulus.body: Source note: Rank-size predicts population proportional to 1/rank. This is the claim the evidence in the topic supports.

questions.stem: A document on testing a rank-size pattern against a table reads: "Rank-size predicts population proportional to 1/rank" Using that evidence, a table lists city populations by rank; what does rank-size predict?

options.text: Rank-size predicts population proportional to 1/rank.
It predicts equal population for all ranks.
options.misconception: mistakes It predicts equal population for all ranks for Rank-size predicts population proportional to 1/rank.

options.text: It predicts growth only for top cities.
It predicts random population order.
options.misconception: confuses It predicts random population order with the supported claim Rank-size predicts population proportional to 1/rank.

questions.explanation: Rank-size predicts population inversely proportional to rank. Equal sizes, top-only growth, or randomness are not the rule.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Rank-size index at a single rank
questions.learningObjective: Explain a rank-size index at one rank
questions.stem: At rank 3, actual population is 320000 and predicted is 333333; what does the index show?

options.text: It measures only total city count.
The index compares actual population to the rank-size prediction.
It is the city's rank alone.
It measures land area of the city.

questions.explanation: The rank-size index compares actual population with the value predicted by the rank-size rule. Rank alone, city count, or land area do not measure fit.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What the rank-size rule assumes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the rank-size rule assumes

stimulus.body: Source note: It assumes a regular hierarchy with constant scaling across ranks. This is the claim the evidence in the topic supports.

questions.stem: A document on what the rank-size rule assumes reads: "It assumes a regular hierarchy with constant scaling across ranks" Using that evidence, a rank-size rule is applied to a city system; what does it assume?

options.text: It assumes only one primate city exists.
It assumes all cities are the same size.
options.misconception: mistakes It assumes all cities are the same size for It assumes a regular hierarchy with constant scaling across….

options.text: It assumes a regular hierarchy with constant scaling across ranks.
It assumes no migration occurs.
options.misconception: adds migration assumption not in rule

questions.explanation: Rank-size assumes a regular hierarchical system with consistent scaling between ranks. Equal sizes, primacy, or migration are not its core assumption.

questions.topic: Rank-size index at a single rank
questions.learningObjective: Explain a rank-size index at one rank
questions.stem: In a worked example about rank-size index at a single rank, at rank 3, actual population is 320000 and predicted is 333333; what does the index show?

answer.exemplar: The index near 0.96 shows the city is slightly smaller than the rank-size prediction, indicating a close but not exact fit to the rule.

questions.explanation: The rank-size index compares actual population with the value predicted by the rank-size rule. Rank alone, city count, or land area do not measure fit.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What counts as an urban place
questions.learningObjective: Define what counts as an urban place

stimulus.body: A clinician's note describes a settlement with dense housing, paved streets, and non-farm employment, but no city charter. It asks whether the settlement is urban.

questions.stem: A note about what counts as an urban place says: "An urban place is defined by population density and built-up land" Against that evidence, where density and built-up land matter, does it count as urban?

options.text: Any settlement with a mayor counts as urban.
Only national capitals are urban.
An urban place is defined by population density and built-up land.
Rural villages with farms are urban.

questions.explanation: Urban status usually depends on density and built-up land, not on governance, capital status, or rural functions. A village with farms remains rural.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Urban area and metropolitan area
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish urban area from metropolitan area
questions.stem: In a worked example about urban area and metropolitan area, a map shows contiguous built-up land and a wider commuting zone; which is the metropolitan area?

options.text: Metropolitan area excludes suburbs.
They are always the same boundary.
Urban area includes all commuting zones.
options.misconception: reads the evidence as Urban area includes all commuting zones instead of Urban area is contiguous built-up land; metropolitan area….

options.text: Urban area is contiguous built-up land; metropolitan area includes commuting ties.

questions.explanation: The urban area covers contiguous built-up land, while the metropolitan area adds commuting and economic ties. They are not automatically the same.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Average annual urban growth rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain average annual urban growth rate
questions.stem: A comparison centered on average annual urban growth rate shows that an urban population rises from 80000 to 128000 over 5 years; what is the growth rate concept?

answer.exemplar: The average annual growth rate is the compound rate that turns 80000 into 128000 over 5 years, not a simple average of yearly increases.

questions.explanation: Average annual growth uses compound growth between the initial and final populations. Simple division or birth rate alone would misstate the rate.
questions.hint: Use compound growth over the period.
